event: Nala answers him: her name is Nala, and she is from very far away.
She says she is not sure how she came here or even what here is, and asks them to set her right.
Jory lets her finish before he speaks; Wat turns his good ear towards her.
Jory answers her politely, and does not ask her twice about far away.
He tells her she is on the Carrow, which they call the Big Water, at the south edge of the Weald.
He reckons by burns and ridges, not miles: the Weald runs days north of here, all pine and hill.
West down the water lies Wenmarch, the town, and south across the river the Crown's country.
North above the pines are the Bare Backs, and he says plainly that nothing lives up there.
Wat puts in that the wolves hold the middle of the Weald, and nobody crosses it after dark.
Wat says the bear came down off the fells this autumn; the east slopes are no place alone.
He says the nearest who can do for a hurt foot is the herb-wife at Brackenford, half a day down.
Jory says the raft will not go down till the burn is out, and that is five days off.
Wat takes her cut foot onto his knee and works pine-tip salve into it with a hard thumb.
It stings like fire, and then the foot is easier than it has been all day.
He wraps it in cloth, and says she will not wear that out in a morning's walking.
Jory pulls his shovel onto his shoulder and goes back out to tend the clamp.
At the doorway he says the gate at Brackenford will want a name, a village and a road.
He says a stranger with no village is held a runaway there, as one plain thing among others.
Wat spits into the fire and looks at her across it for a while.
He asks her straight out, the way he would ask about weather, whether anybody is hunting her.
